title: Ice Cream 1.5L

drivers.name: Price increase + new competitor
drivers.evidence: Price rose 2.3% vs regular; same week last year (2025-09-28) saw 24 units after a 2.3% price hike, down from baseline. New competitor across the street increases substitution risk. Past promotions show noise-adjusted lift of x1.25, but deeper discounts than this. This week combines a price increase

adjustment.analysis: Halloween has negligible historical lift (noise-adjusted x1.0). The 2.3% price increase is likely to suppress demand, especially with a new competitor across the street. Past promotions show a median lift of x1.25 (noise-adjusted), but this price increase exceeds prior discounts and coincides with a new competitive threat. The combination suggests demand erosion. The baseline's recent weeks show no trend, and the prior promotion week (2026-09-28) saw a drop to 24 units after a price hike, supporting a downside effect. The classical model's neutral suggestion is overridden by context.

PRODUCT: Ice Cream 1.5L | category Frozen | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-10-26 to 2026-11-01 (3 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: Holiday: Halloween (Sat)
  shelf price: 6.56 (+2.3% vs regular price 6.41)
  planner notes: A competitor opens a store across the street this week

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 44.6 | 5%-95%: 17.1 - 70.6 | 10%-90%: 24.4 - 66.9

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-36% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
